feature1.prompt: Changing a user's email should invalidate any previously generated password reset token. In the current flow, a user with an email such as foo@… requests a password reset, but if they change their email before using the reset link, the token is still accepted. The intended fix is to update the token generation logic so that the current email is factored into the hash. In particular, PasswordResetTokenGenerator._make_hash_value() must be modified to include the user’s email, ensuring that any change to the email address will result in a different token value.
feature1.hint_texts: This feature focuses exclusively on updating the token generation logic. The developer should retrieve the user’s email by using the model’s get_email_field_name() method and include its value (defaulting to an empty string if not present) into the hashed output. The change must be isolated within django/contrib/auth/tokens.py so that tokens generated when the email is unchanged remain compatible with existing behavior.
feature1.entrypoint: File: django/contrib/auth/tokens.py; Method: _make_hash_value. The modification should occur near the return statement where user.pk, password, and login timestamp are concatenated. The email should be fetched via user.get_email_field_name() and appended to the hash string.

feature2.prompt: Changing a user's email should invalidate any previously generated password reset token. In the outlined scenario, even though a password reset request was made using an original email address, the token must be rejected if the user subsequently updates their email address. The solution must therefore guarantee that the token reflects the current email value and that using an outdated email produces an invalid token. This requirement calls for adjustments in the models and tests to verify that the token becomes invalid when the email is changed.
feature2.hint_texts: This feature covers the enhancements in the testing apparatus and model adjustments needed to validate the new token behavior. Developers need to update the test models so that a CustomEmailField (with a nullable email field) is properly supported, and ensure that changes in the user’s email are detected as part of token generation. The test enhancements include adding a test case that verifies that when the email is changed, the previously generated token is rejected, and related test files in the auth_tests directory must be modified accordingly.
feature2.entrypoint: Test files to modify include: tests/auth_tests/models/__init__.py, tests/auth_tests/models/with_custom_email_field.py, tests/auth_tests/test_models.py, and tests/auth_tests/test_tokens.py. In particular, focus on the new CustomEmailField model adjustments and the new test method (test_token_with_different_email) that checks token invalidation when the email changes.

collaboration_points.shared_resources: Both features rely on the PasswordResetTokenGenerator in django/contrib/auth/tokens.py as well as shared user model components (including the CustomEmailField) and related test files in the auth_tests directory.
collaboration_points.integration_strategy: Feature1 exposes an updated token generation API that now factors in the user's email address. Feature2 provides comprehensive tests and model adjustments to verify the new behavior. Integration requires that the token logic change and the new tests work in harmony to ensure that tokens become invalid once a user’s email changes.
collaboration_points.communication_needs: Developers should coordinate on the expected behavior of the updated _make_hash_value() method and agree on how the CustomEmailField should behave when the email is null or modified. Regular discussions are recommended to ensure that the test enhancements accurately capture the edge cases and that any shared interfaces between the token generator and user model remain consistent.
